**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 36, verses 5–8:**

﴿Revelation from the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "تَنْزِيلَ" (*tanzīla*) with a fatha on the lām, as if he had said: "He sent down a sending down" (*nuzzila tanzīlan*). The others read it with a damma (*tanzīlu*), meaning: "It is the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

﴿So that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless.﴾ It has been said that "مَا" (*mā*) here is negative, meaning: their fathers were not warned, because Quraysh had not been visited by any prophet before Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that "مَا" means "the one who" (*alladhī*), meaning: so that you may warn a people with that with which their fathers were warned. ﴿So they are heedless﴾ of faith and right guidance.

﴿Indeed the word has come into effect﴾, meaning the punishment has become due, ﴿upon most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ This is like His saying: ﴿But the word of punishment has come into effect upon the disbelievers﴾ [az-Zumar: 71].

﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks﴾. It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his two companions from the Banu Makhzum. The reason was that Abu Jahl had sworn that if he saw Muhammad praying he would crush his head. So he came to him while he was praying, carrying a stone to smash him with. When he raised it, his hand became stuck to his neck and the stone clung to his hand. When he returned to his companions and told them what he had seen, the stone fell off. A man from the Banu Makhzum said: "I will kill him with this stone." So he came to him while he was praying, to throw the stone at him, but Allah the Exalted blinded his sight, so he began to hear his voice but not see him. He returned to his companions and could not see them until they called out to him. They said to him: "What did you do?" He said: "I did not see him, but I heard his voice, and something came between me and him like a stallion swishing its tail [[yakhtur: a camel raises its tail again and again and strikes its thighs with it]], and if I had come near him it would have eaten me." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks﴾. (Narrated by al-Tabari in abridged form, 22/152. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajr said in al-Kafi al-Shaf, p. 139: "Ibn Ishaq narrated it in his Sira, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, through Ibn Ishaq: 'Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id, or Ikrimah, related to me from Ibn 'Abbas, up to his words: his hands became stuck to the stone...' Its original form is in al-Bukhari through Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both." See also Ibn Kathir 3/565 and al-Bahr al-Muhit 7/324.)

The scholars of the meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: this is by way of metaphor, and there were no actual shackles. The intended meaning is: We prevented them from faith by obstacles, and so We made the shackles an image for that. al-Farra' said: its meaning is that We held them back from spending in the way of Allah, like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29], meaning: do not withhold it from spending.

﴿So they are up to their chins﴾. "هِيَ" (*hiya*, "they") is a pronoun referring to the hands, even though they have not been mentioned, because the shackle binds the hand to the neck. The meaning is: We placed shackles on their hands and necks, so they are up to their chins. ﴿So they are raised-headed﴾. "المُقْمَحُ" (*al-muqmah*) is one whose head is raised and whose gaze is lowered. It is said: "a camel is *qāmih*" when it has drunk its fill of water, and then "*aqmaha*" when it raises its head and lowers its gaze. al-Azhari said: he meant that when their hands were chained to their necks, the shackles lifted their chins and heads, so they are raised-headed because the shackles raise them.

**Al-Baghawi's commentary (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 36, verse 13:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Set forth to them the parable of the people of the town﴾. That is, mention to them a comparison, similar to their own situation, from the story of the companions of the town, which is Antioch (Antakiya). ﴿When the messengers came to it﴾, that is, the messengers of Jesus, upon him be peace.

The scholars of the reports about the prophets (al-'ulama bi-akhbar al-anbiya') said: Jesus sent two messengers from among the disciples (al-hawariyyun) to the people of the city of Antioch.[[Ibn Kathir said (3/570): "It has been mentioned earlier that many of the early generation (al-salaf) held that this town was Antioch, and that these three were messengers of the Messiah Jesus son of Mary, upon him be peace, as Qatada and others stated. This is the view that none of the later exegetes has reported except him, and there is room for doubt about it on several grounds. (First) The apparent meaning of the story indicates that these were messengers of God, the Mighty and Majestic, not from the Messiah, upon him be peace, as God the Exalted says: ‘When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened them with a third, and they said: Indeed we are messengers to you… Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you. And we are only responsible for clear conveyance.’ Had these been disciples, they would have used an expression indicating that they were from the Messiah, upon him be peace, and God knows best. Moreover, if they had been messengers of the Messiah, they would not have said to them: ‘You are only human like us.’ (Second) The people of Antioch believed in the messengers of the Messiah sent to them, and they were the first city to believe in the Messiah. For this reason, among the Christians it was one of the four cities that have patriarchs: Jerusalem, because it is the city of the Messiah; Antioch, because it was the first town to believe in the Messiah, according to its last people; Alexandria, because there they agreed to establish the patriarchs, metropolitans, bishops, priests, deacons and monks; and then Rome, because it is the city of King Constantine, who supported their religion and established it. (Third) The story of Antioch with the disciples, the companions of the Messiah, occurred after the revelation of the Torah." See also al-Muharrar al-Wajiz by Ibn Atiyya, 13/193.]] When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending his small flock, and he was Habib the carpenter, the companion of Ya-Sin.[[In "B": Isa.]] They greeted him, and the old man said to them: "Who are you?" They said: "We are the messengers of Jesus. We call you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes. We heal the sick, and by God's permission we cure the blind and the leper." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill for years." They said: "Come, let us go and look at his condition." So he brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and he stood up at once, healthy, by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God the Exalted healed many of the sick through their hands. Their king, whom Wahb said was named Antiyakhus, was one of the kings of the Romans and worshipped idols. They said: "The news reached him, so he summoned them and said: 'Who are you?' They said: 'We are the messengers of Jesus.' He said: 'And why have you come?' They said: 'We call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees.' He said: 'Do you have a god other than our gods?' They said: 'Yes, the One who created you and your gods.' He said: 'Stand up until I consider your matter.' The people followed them, seized them and beat them in the marketplace."

Wahb said: Jesus sent these two men to Antioch. They came to it but could not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they proclaimed God's greatness and remembered God. The king became angry, ordered them imprisoned, and each of them was flogged one hundred lashes. They said: When the two messengers were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the leader of the disciples, Shim'un al-Safa (Simon Peter), after them to support them. Shim'un entered the city disguised, and he began to associate with the king's courtiers until they became fond of him. They reported his news to the king, who summoned him. The king was pleased with his company, became fond of him and honoured him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to a religion other than yours. Have you spoken with them and heard what they say?" The king said: "Anger has prevented me from that." He said: "If the king sees fit, let him summon them so that we may learn what they have." The king summoned them. Shim'un said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'un said to them: "Describe Him concisely." They said: "He does what He wills and decrees what He desires." Shim'un said: "And what is your sign?"[[Omitted from "A": what is between the brackets.]] They said: "Whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes had been effaced, the place of his eyes being like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight split open. They then took two pellets of clay[[Al-bunduqiyya: what is rounded out of clay.]] and placed them in his eyeballs, and they became two eyes with which he could see. The king marvelled, and Shim'un said to the king: "If you were to ask your god to do a deed like this, the honour would be yours and your god's." The king said: "I have no secret from you. Our god, whom we worship, neither hears nor sees, nor does harm or good." Whenever the king entered the idol's temple, Shim'un would enter with him, pray much and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed. The king said to the two messengers: "If your god whom you worship is able to revive a dead person, we will believe in him and in you." They said: "Our God is capable of everything." The king said: "Here is a dead person who died seven days ago, the son of a landowner. I delayed burying him until his father returned, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, now changed and foul-smelling. The two messengers began to call upon their Lord openly, and Shim'un called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I came seven days ago as a polytheist, and I was made to enter seven valleys of fire. I warn you of what you are in, so believe in God." Then he said: "The doors of heaven were opened to me, and I looked and saw a handsome young man interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'un and these two," pointing to his two companions. The king marvelled. When Shim'un knew that his words had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and called him to faith. The king believed, a group of people believed, and others disbelieved.

It is also said: A daughter of the king had died and been buried. Shim'un said to the king: "Ask these two men to revive your daughter." The king asked them to do so. They stood, prayed and called upon God, with Shim'un praying with them in secret. God revived the woman, the grave split open, and she came out. She said: "Submit, for these two are truthful." She said: "I do not think you will submit." Then she asked the two messengers to return her to her place, so they threw dust on her head, and she returned to her grave as she had been.

Ibn Ishaq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people resolved to kill the messengers. This reached Habib, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the messengers. This is the meaning of His saying, the Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 14:

﴿When We sent to them two messengers﴾. Wahb said: "Their names were Yuhanna (John) and Bulus (Paul)." ﴿But they denied them, so We strengthened﴾, meaning: We reinforced, ﴿with a third﴾, with a third messenger, who was Sham'un (Simon). Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light (takhfif) pronunciation, and it has the same meaning as the first, like your saying: shaddadnā and shaddadnā (with light and heavy pronunciation). It was also said: meaning "fa-ghalabnā" (We overpowered), from their saying: "Whoever is mighty plunders" (man 'azza bazz). Ka'b said: "The two messengers were Sadiq and Sadduq, and the third was Shalum." God attributed the sending to Himself because 'Isa, peace be upon him, sent them only by the command of God, the Exalted. ﴿They said﴾, all of them, to the people of Antioch: ﴿Indeed, we are sent to you﴾.

﴿They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing. You are only lying."﴾ "You are only liars in what you claim."

﴿They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you."﴾

﴿And our duty is only clear conveyance.﴾

﴿They said: "Indeed, we take omen from you."﴾ i.e., we consider you a bad omen (tasha'amna bikum). The reason was that rain had been withheld from them, so they said: "This has befallen us because of your ill omen." ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you﴾, i.e., we will surely kill you. Qatadah said: "By stoning." ﴿And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us.﴾

﴿They said: "Your omen is with you."﴾ i.e., your ill omen is with you, because of your disbelief and denial; that is, the ill omen has befallen you from your own side. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "Your share of good and evil." ﴿Is it because you are reminded?﴾ i.e., because you have been admonished with Allah? Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 25–29:

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ Meaning: listen to me. When he said that, the people rushed at him as one man and killed him [[Narrated by Ibn Ishaq as a mursal report from Ibn ʿAbbas, Kaʿb, and Wahb. See: Ibn Kathir: 3 / 569.]].

Ibn Masʿud said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 22 / 161, and Ibn Ishaq from some of his companions from Ibn Masʿud. See Ibn Kathir: 3 / 569.]].

Al-Suddi said: They were pelting him with stones while he was saying, "O Allah, guide my people," until they cut him to pieces and killed him [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 22 / 161, but from Qatada; likewise in Ibn Kathir: 3 / 569.]].

Al-Hasan said: They made a hole in a ring and tied him by it to one of the walls of the city, and his grave is in Antioch. Allah admitted him into Paradise while he was alive there, receiving provision. This is the meaning of His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise.﴾ When he reached Paradise, ﴿he said: Would that my people knew of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored.﴾ Meaning: by my Lord's forgiveness of me. ﴿And made me among the honored﴾: he wished that his people would know that Allah had forgiven him and honored him, so that they would be drawn to the religion of the messengers.

When Habib was killed, Allah became angry on his behalf and hastened punishment upon them. He commanded Jibril, peace be upon him, who cried out at them with a single cry, and they all died to the last one. This is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven﴾, meaning: the angels, ﴿nor were We ever sending down﴾, meaning: We were not going to do this; rather, the matter of their destruction was easier than they imagined.

It was also said: the meaning of "And We did not send down upon his people after him" is: upon the people of Habib the carpenter, after his killing, any host, and We were not going to send them down upon the nations when We destroyed them, such as the flood, the thunderbolt, and the wind. Then He explained their punishment, saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was but one cry﴾, [and Abu Jaʿfar read: "ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun" with a raised ending] [[What is between the brackets is missing from "A".]], with the raising, making the "kawn" (being) mean "occurrence" (wuqūʿ).

The exegetes said: Jibril took hold of the two doorposts (ʿiḍādatā) of the city gate, then cried out at them with a single cry [[Mentioned by Ibn Kathir: 3 / 570. ʿIḍādatā al-bāb: its two sides.]], ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾, meaning dead.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 39–40:

﴿And the moon — We have determined for it phases﴾. That is, We have determined for it phases (manazil). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and the people of Basra read "al-qamaru" (the moon) with a *damma* on the *ra'*, based on His saying: "And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day." The others read it with a *fatha* (*naṣb*), based on His saying "We have determined it," meaning: We have determined the moon ﴿phases﴾. We have already mentioned the names of the lunar phases (manazil) in surah Yunus [[See above: 4/121.]]. When the moon reaches the last of its phases, it becomes thin, and this is His saying: ﴿until it returns like the old dry palm stalk﴾. The *'urjun* (dry palm stalk) is the *'ud al-'idhq* [[In manuscript A: al-'irq.]], the stem of the date cluster that bears the *shamarikh* (the strands of the cluster). When it becomes old and ages, it dries out, bends, and turns yellow. So the moon, in its thinness and yellowness at the end of its phases, is likened to it.

﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾. That is, the day does not enter upon the night before the night has ended, and the night does not enter upon the day before the day has ended. This is His exalted saying: ﴿nor does the night outrun the day﴾, meaning: they alternate in a known reckoning, and neither of them comes before its time.

It has also been said: neither of them enters into the domain of the other. The sun does not rise at night, and the moon does not rise by day while it still has its light. If the two were to meet, and each were to overtake the other, the Resurrection would take place.

It has also been said: ﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, meaning: they do not come together in one orbit. ﴿Nor does the night outrun the day﴾, meaning: one night does not follow directly upon another night without a day separating them.

﴿Each is travelling in an orbit (falak)﴾: they glide (yajrun).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 41–45:

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾. Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham, and Ya'qub recited "dhurriyyatihim" (in the plural, "their offspring"), as a plural form. The others recited "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Whoever read it in the plural put a kasra on the taa' (ta), and whoever read it in the singular put a fatha on it (nasb). The intended meaning of "dhurriyyah" (offspring) is the forefathers and ancestors, and the term dhurriyyah applies to forefathers just as it applies to children. ﴿In the laden ship﴾, that is, the filled one. He meant the ship of Nuh (peace be upon him), and these people were from the descendants of those who were carried with Nuh, and they were in their loins.

﴿And We created for them of its like that which they ride﴾. It was said: he meant by this the small ships which were built after the ship of Nuh in its form.

It was also said: he meant by this the ships that sail on the rivers; so they on the rivers are like the great ships on the seas. This is the saying of Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and others.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "And We created for them of its like that which they ride" means: the camels, for the camels on land are like ships on the sea.

﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no outcry﴾, that is, no helper ﴿for them, nor are they rescued﴾, that is, they are not saved from drowning. Ibn 'Abbas said: and no one rescues them from My punishment.

﴿Except as a mercy from Us and a provision for a time﴾, until the end of their appointed terms; meaning, except that He shows them mercy and lets them enjoy life until their appointed times.

﴿And when it is said to them: Beware what is before you and what is behind you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is before you" means the Hereafter, so act for it; "and what is behind you" means this world, so beware of it and do not be deceived by it.

It was also said: "What is before you" refers to the events of Allah concerning the nations who came before you, and "what is behind you" refers to the punishment of the Hereafter. This is the saying of Qatadah and Muqatil.

﴿That you may receive mercy﴾. The answer (jawab) is omitted, and its estimated form is: when it is said to them this, they turn away from it; its evidence is what follows it.

The commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on Surah 36, verses 46–49:

﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord﴾, i.e., an evidence of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you"﴾, i.e., has given you, ﴿those who disbelieved say to those who believe, "Shall we feed﴾, i.e., shall we provide sustenance to, ﴿whom, if God willed, He would have fed?"﴾ This is because the believers said to the disbelievers of Makkah: "Spend on the needy from the wealth which you claim belongs to God," meaning what they had set aside for God from their crops and livestock. They replied: "Shall we feed whom, if God willed, He would have provided for, and then He did not provide for him despite His power over it? We agree with the will of God, so we will not feed whom God has not fed." This is something the miserly cling to; they say: "We do not give to whom God has deprived." But what they claim is false, because God made some of creation wealthy and made some of them poor as a trial. He withheld the world from the poor, not out of stinginess, and He commanded the wealthy to spend, not because He needed their wealth; rather, He tests the wealthy through the poor in what He has enjoined upon them regarding the wealth of the rich. No one has any objection to the will of God or His judgment concerning His creation. ﴿You are only in manifest error﴾. The disbelievers say to the believers: "You are only in clear error in following Muhammad (ﷺ) and abandoning what we are upon."

﴿And they say, "When is this promise"﴾, i.e., the Resurrection and the Raising, ﴿if you are truthful?"﴾

God the Exalted said: ﴿They await nothing﴾, i.e., they do not wait for anything, ﴿but a single blast﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the first blast (of the trumpet). ﴿It will seize them while they are disputing﴾, meaning: they will be quarrelling about worldly matters, such as buying and selling, and talking in gatherings and markets.

Hamzah recited "yakhishimun" (يَخِصِّمُونَ) with a sukun on the kha' and a lightened sad, meaning: some of them overcome others in quarrelling. The others recited it with a shaddah on the sad, meaning: they quarrel (yakhtasimun), the ta' being assimilated into the sad (idgham, assimilation of consonants). Then Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub and Warsh pronounce the kha' with a fatha, transferring the vowel of the assimilated ta' to it; Abu Ja'far and Qalun pronounce it with a sukun, and Abu 'Amr pronounces it with an intended (rawm) fatha on the kha' [93a]. The rest recited it with a kasra on the kha'.

It has been related to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly come while two men have spread their garment between them, and they will neither complete a sale nor fold it. The Hour will certainly come while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, and he will not eat it."

[Fragment of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in *al-Fitan* 13/81–82, and by the author in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 15/26–27.]

**Verse 54–58**

﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in delight.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "fi shughlin" with the ghayn unvowelled (sukun), while the rest read it with a damma. Both are dialectal variants (lughatan), like al-suht and al-suhut.

The scholars differed over the meaning of ash-shughl (busyness, occupation). Ibn 'Abbas said: "In deflowering the virgins."[[Narrated by al-Tabari, 23/18. al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur 7/64, also attributes it to Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Jannah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh.]] Waki' ibn al-Jarrah said: "In listening (to music)."

al-Kalbi said: "Busy with (delight), away from the people of the Fire and from what they are in. Their affairs do not concern them, and they do not remember them."

al-Hasan said: "They are occupied with the bliss that is in the Garden, away from the torment in which the people of the Fire are."

Ibn Kaysan said: "In visiting one another." It is also said: "In the hospitality of Allah the Exalted."[[See these opinions in al-Bahr al-Muhit 7/342.]]

﴿fakihun﴾ (jesting, rejoicing). Abu Ja'far read "fakihun" wherever it occurs, and Hafs agreed with him in al-Mutaffifin. Both are dialectal variants, like al-hadhir and al-hadhir, meaning: pleasantly situated (na'imun). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "Pleased with what they are in." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Joyful."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 66–67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ [i.e., We would have removed their eyes] [[What is between the brackets is an addition from "b".]] the visible ones, such that no eyelid or slit would appear on them, and this is the meaning of ṭams (obliteration), as Allah, exalted is He, said: "And if Allah had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight" [al-Baqarah: 20]. He says: just as We blinded their hearts, if We willed We would have blinded their visible eyes. ﴿So they would race to the path﴾ i.e., hasten toward the way. ﴿But how could they see?﴾ i.e., how could they see [and We had blinded their eyes? That is: if We willed, We would have led them astray from guidance and left them blind, wandering, so how could they see] [[What is between the brackets is omitted from "a".]] the path at that time? This is the saying of al-Hasan and al-Suddi. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Muqatil and 'Ata' said: its meaning is, if We willed, We would have gouged out the eyes of their misguidance, so We would have blinded them to their error, and turned their sight from misguidance to guidance so that they would see their right course. ﴿But how could they see?﴾ And I did not do that to them?

﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ meaning: their places. He intends: if We willed, We would have made them apes and swine in their dwellings. It is also said: if We willed, We would have made them stones while they sat in their dwellings with no spirits in them.

﴿So they would not be able to proceed, nor would they return﴾ to what they had been upon. It is also said: they would not be able to go forward or to return.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 68–69:**

﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation.﴾ ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read "نُنَكِّسُهُ" with a shaddah (doubled letter). The others read it with a fatḥah on the first nūn and a ḍammah on the kāf, without the shaddah (the two are different recitations, qirāʾāt). The meaning is: We return him to the lowest point of life, like a child at the beginning of creation.

It was also said: "نُنَكِّسُهُ فِي الْخَلْقِ" means: We weaken his limbs after their strength, and return them to their deficiency after their growth.

﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ So that they may take heed and know that the One who has power to turn the states of a human being has power to resurrect him after death.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him.﴾ Al-Kalbī said: The disbelievers of Makkah said, "Muḥammad is a poet, and what he recites is poetry." So Allah revealed, refuting them: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him.﴾ That is: it was not easy for him, and no line of poetry would come out metrically correct for him. When he quoted a line of poetry, it came out of his tongue broken.

Abū Saʿīd al-Shurayḥī told us, Abū Isḥāq al-Thaʿlabī told us, al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Thaqafī told me, Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Ḥamdān told us, Yūsuf ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Māhān told us, Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl told us, Ḥammād ibn Salamah told us, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from al-Ḥasan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to quote this line: "Islam and white hair suffice a man as a restrainer."

Abū Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, the poet only said: 'White hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer.'"[[The line belongs to Suḥaym ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥashās, and its first half is: "ʿUmayrah, leave off, if you have readied yourself as a raider." See al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Bayān wa'l-Tabyīn: 1/71; al-Mubarrad, al-Kāmil, p. 585; and Ibn Kathīr's tafsir: 7/574, Shaʿb edition.]]

[And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saying: "Islam and white hair suffice a man as a restrainer."] Then Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him.﴾"[[Related by Ibn Saʿd: 1/382–383 (the words between the brackets we have supplemented from it). al-Suyūṭī, in al-Durr al-Manthūr: 7/71, attributes it to Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Marzubānī in Muʿjam al-Shuʿarāʾ. ʿAlī ibn Zayd is weak.]]

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Malīḥī told us, Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Shurayḥ told us, Abū al-Qāsim al-Baghawī told us, ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd told us, Sharīk told us, from al-Miqdām ibn Shurayḥ, from his father, who said: I said to ʿĀʾishah: "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) quote any poetry?" She said: "He used to quote from the poetry of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah."

She said: "And sometimes he would say: 'And there comes to you with news one whom you did not provide for.'"[[Related by al-Tirmidhī in al-Adab, chapter: What has come concerning reciting poetry: 8/140–141, and he said: "This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth." Also by Aḥmad: 6/156, and Ibn Saʿd: 1/383. Ibn Kathīr (3/579) also attributes it to al-Nasāʾī.]]

Maʿmar said, from Qatādah: "It reached me that ʿĀʾishah was asked: 'Did the Prophet (ﷺ) quote any poetry?' She said: 'Poetry was the most hateful speech to him.' **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 36, verses 78–82**

﴿And he made for Us a parable and forgot his own creation.﴾ That is, the beginning of his own origin. Then ﴿he said, "Who will give life to these bones when they are decayed?"﴾ That is, crumbled to dust. He did not say *ramīmah* (رَمِيمَةً) because it is *ma'dūl* (مَعْدُولٌ, "diverted from its original form") from *fā'ilah* (فَاعِلَةٍ). Whatever is diverted from its original form and pattern is treated differently from its counterparts. [[In "A": its *i'rāb* (إعرابه, grammatical inflection).]] Compare His saying, ﴿"Your mother was not unchaste (*baghiyyan*)"﴾ [Maryam: 28], where the *hā'* (ه) is dropped because the word has been diverted from *bāghiyah* (بَاغِيَةٍ).

﴿Say, "He will give them life who brought them into being the first time, and He is Knower of every creation."﴾ That is, who created them.

﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: these are two trees, one called *al-Markh* (الْمَرْخُ) and the other *al-Afar* (الْعَفَارُ). Whoever among them wanted fire would cut two branches from them, like two siwak sticks, and they are green, with water dripping from them. Then *al-Markh* is rubbed against *al-Afar*, and fire comes out of them by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. [[See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/583; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 7/348.]]

The Arabs say: "In every tree there is fire," and *al-Markh* and *al-Afar* are famous for it. The sages (*al-hukama'*) said: "In every tree there is fire, except *al-'Unnab*."

﴿Then, behold, you kindle (fire) from it﴾, that is, you strike and kindle fire from that tree. Then He mentioned what is greater than the creation of man, saying:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ Ya'qub read *yaqdir* (يَقْدِرُ) with the *yā'* (ي), treating it as a verb. ﴿"Yes," (say, "Yes")﴾, that is, say: "Yes, He is able to do that." ﴿And He is the Creator, the Knower﴾ [He creates creation after creation], ﴿the Knower﴾ of all that He has created.
